title: Python Data Structures and OOP
summary: Data structures determine how you store and access information efficiently, while object-oriented programming lets you model real-world entities as reusable objects with data and behavior. Most AI libraries are built with OOP, so understanding classe
content:
# Python Data Structures and OOP ##### The lookup that took eleven minutes A student wrote a script to match 20,000 customer records against a list of 5,000 fraudulent account IDs. The logic was correct and the code was readable: ```python fraud_ids = [4471, 8823, 1092, ...] # a list of 5,000 IDs for customer in customers: # 20,000 customers if customer["account_id"] in fraud_ids: # scans the list, item by item flag(customer) ``` It took eleven minutes. Changing one character — the brackets on `fraud_ids` from `[` to `{` — brought it to under a second. The reason is structural. Checking `in` on a **list** scans every element until it finds a match: 20,000 × up to 5,000 comparisons is 100 million operations. Checking `in` on a **set** uses hashing to jump straight to the answer, regardless of size. Choosing the right data structure is not a stylistic preference. It is often the difference between a script that finishes and one that does not — and it is the first place where knowing *why* Python behaves as it does pays off directly. ##### The four core structures | | Syntax | Ordered | Mutable | Duplicates | `in` speed | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | **List** | `[1, 2, 3]` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Slow — O(n) | | **Tuple** | `(1, 2, 3)` | Yes | **No** | Yes | Slow — O(n) | | **Set** | `{1, 2, 3}` | No | Yes | **No** | **Fast — O(1)** | | **Dict** | `{"a": 1}` | Yes* | Yes | Keys unique | **Fast — O(1)** | *Dictionaries preserve insertion order in Python 3.7+. **Lists** are your default ordered collection — a dataset of records, a sequence of losses, a batch of predictions. ```python losses = [0.92, 0.61, 0.44, 0.38] losses.append(0.35) # add to the end losses.insert(0, 1.10) # insert at a position print(losses[-1]) # 0.35 — negative indexes count from the end print(losses[1:3]) # [0.92, 0.61] — slicing print(sorted(losses)) # a new sorted list losses.sort() # sorts in place, returns None ``` That last distinction bites people: `sorted(x)` returns a new list; `x.sort()` modifies `x` and returns `None`. Writing `losses = losses.sort()` silently sets `losses` to `None`. **Tuples** are immutable — use them for fixed groupings and for values that must not change: ```python image_shape = (224, 224, 3) # height, width, channels height, width, channels = image_shape # unpacking # Immutability means tuples can be dictionary keys; lists cannot cache = {(0, 0): "top-left", (1, 1): "centre"} ``` **Sets** hold unique items with fast membership testing and set algebra: ```python train_ids = {101, 102, 103, 104} test_ids = {103, 104, 105} print(train_ids & test_ids) # {103, 104} — intersection: DATA LEAKAGE! print(train_ids | test_ids) # union print(train_ids - test_ids) # {101, 102} — difference ``` That intersection check is a genuinely useful habit: if your training and test IDs overlap, your evaluation is meaningless. One line catches it. **Dictionaries** map keys to values, and they are the workhorse of AI code — configurations, label mappings, JSON payloads, model metrics: ```python config = {"model": "resnet50", "epochs": 30, "lr": 0.001} print(config["model"]) # KeyError if absent print(config.get("batch_size", 32)) # 32 — safe access with a default config["batch_size"] = 64 # add or update for key, value in config.items(): print(f"{key}: {value}") ``` **`.get()` with a default should be your habit.** Real data has missing fields, and `dict[key]` crashes on the first one. ##### Comprehensions Comprehensions build a new collection from an existing one in a single expression. They are idiomatic Python, and you will see them everywhere in ML code. ```python scores = [88, 42, 95, 67, 73, 31] # map: transform every element normalized = [s / 100 for s in scores] # filter: keep some elements passing = [s for s in scores if s >= 60] # map + filter together scaled_passing = [s / 100 for s in scores if s >= 60] # with an index labelled = [f"student_{i}: {s}" for i, s in enumerate(scores)] ``` The equivalent loop for the third example is four lines with a `result = []` and an `append`. The comprehension is one, and once your eye is trained it is easier to read. Dictionary and set comprehensions follow the same pattern: ```python classes = ["cat", "dog", "bird", "fish"] label_to_idx = {label: i for i, label in enumerate(classes)} # {'cat': 0, 'dog': 1, 'bird': 2, 'fish': 3} idx_to_label = {i: label for label, i in label_to_idx.items()} # invert it unique_lengths = {len(c) for c in classes} # {3, 4} ``` That `label_to_idx` / `idx_to_label` pair is exactly what you build for every classification problem — models predict integers, humans read names. One caution: **keep comprehensions to one level.** A nested comprehension with two conditions is harder to read than the loop it replaces. Readability wins. ##### Classes and objects A **class** is a blueprint bundling data (attributes) with behaviour (methods). This matters for AI work because **every major library is object-oriented**: `model.fit()`, `df.groupby()`, `optimizer.step()` are all method calls on objects. ```python class Dataset: """A simple in-memory dataset of records.""" def __init__(self, name: str, records: list[dict] | None = None): self.name = name # instance attributes self.records = records or [] # avoids the mutable-default trap def add(self, record: dict) -> None: """Add one record, validating required fields.""" if not isinstance(record, dict): raise TypeError(f"expected dict, got {type(record).__name__}") if "id" not in record: raise ValueError("record must have an 'id' field") self.records.append(record) def filter(self, **criteria) -> "Dataset": """Return a new Dataset containing records matching all criteria.""" matched = [ r for r in self.records if all(r.get(k) == v for k, v in criteria.items()) ] return Dataset(f"{self.name}_filtered", matched) def summary(self) -> dict: """Basic statistics about the dataset.""" if not self.records: return {"name": self.name, "count": 0} keys = {k for r in self.records for k in r} return { "name": self.name, "count": len(self.records), "fields": sorted(keys), "complete": sum(1 for r in self.records if keys <= set(r)), } def __len__(self) -> int: # enables len(dataset) return len(self.records) def __repr__(self) -> str: # readable output when printed return f"Dataset(name={self.name!r}, records={len(self.records)})" ds = Dataset("iris") ds.add({"id": 1, "species": "setosa", "petal_length": 1.4}) ds.add({"id": 2, "species": "virginica", "petal_length": 5.1}) print(ds) # Dataset(name='iris', records=2) print(len(ds)) # 2 print(ds.filter(species="setosa").summary()) ``` The pieces worth naming. **`__init__`** runs when you create an instance. **`self`** refers to the instance, and every method takes it as its first parameter. **Dunder methods** like `__len__` and `__repr__` hook into Python's built-in behaviour — implementing `__len__` is why `len(ds)` works, and `__repr__` is why printing gives something useful rather than ``. ##### Inheritance **Inheritance** lets a class extend another, reusing its behaviour: ```python class LabelledDataset(Dataset): """A Dataset where every record must carry a label.""" def __init__(self, name: str, label_field: str, records=None): super().__init__(name, records) # run the parent's __init__ self.label_field = label_field def add(self, record: dict) -> None: # override the parent method if self.label_field not in record: raise ValueError(f"record missing label field {self.label_field!r}") super().add(record) # then reuse the parent's logic def class_counts(self) -> dict: # new behaviour counts: dict = {} for r in self.records: label = r[self.label_field] counts[label] = counts.get(label, 0) + 1 return counts train = LabelledDataset("train", label_field="species") train.add({"id": 1, "species": "setosa"}) print(train.class_counts()) # {'setosa': 1} ``` `super()` calls the parent's version, which lets you *extend* rather than *replace* — here, adding a validation check before delegating the actual append. That is exactly how you subclass PyTorch's `Dataset` and `nn.Module` later in this course. A useful design guideline: **prefer composition over inheritance.** Inherit when the child genuinely *is a* kind of the parent; otherwise, hold an object as an attribute instead. Deep inheritance hierarchies become hard to follow quickly. ##### Exception handling Errors are inevitable when reading real data. Handling them deliberately keeps a batch job running. ```python def load_scores(path: str) -> list[float]: scores = [] try: with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f: for line_no, line in enumerate(f, start=1): line = line.strip() if not line: continue try: scores.append(float(line)) except ValueError: print(f"line {line_no}: skipping unparseable value {line!r}") except FileNotFoundError: raise # let the caller decide except PermissionError as exc: raise RuntimeError(f"cannot read {path}") from exc finally: print(f"finished reading {path}") # runs whether or not it failed return scores ``` Three principles there. **Catch specific exceptions** — a bare `except:` swallows `KeyboardInterrupt` and genuine bugs alongside the error you meant to handle. **Handle at the right level**: a bad line is skipped locally, while a missing file propagates to the caller. And **`finally` always runs**, which is where cleanup belongs. Raise your own exceptions when a caller has broken a contract, as `Dataset.add` does above — a clear `ValueError` beats a mysterious failure three functions later. ##### File I/O The `with` statement guarantees the file closes, even if an error occurs: ```python import json, csv # JSON — the format of configs, API responses and metadata with open("config.json", encoding="utf-8") as f: config = json.load(f) with open("results.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f: json.dump({"accuracy": 0.94, "epochs": 30}, f, indent=2) # CSV — DictReader gives you dictionaries keyed by the header row with open("data.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f: rows = list(csv.DictReader(f)) with open("clean.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f: writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=["id", "species", "petal_length"]) writer.writeheader() writer.writerows(rows) ``` Two arguments that are not optional in practice: **`encoding="utf-8"`** (the default differs on Windows and will crash on the first accented character) and **`newline=""`** for CSV writing (without it, Windows inserts a blank line between rows). ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Need a collection?] --> B{Key-value pairs?} B -->|yes| C[dict] B -->|no| D{Fast membership
or dedup needed?} D -->|yes| E[set] D -->|no| F{Must it be
immutable?} F -->|yes| G[tuple] F -->|no| H[list] ``` ##### Common mistakes - **Using a list for membership tests** on large collections — the eleven-minute lookup. - **`dict[key]`** on data that might be missing; use `.get(key, default)`. - **`x = x.sort()`**, which assigns `None`. - **Mutable default arguments** — `records=None` then `records or []`. - **Modifying a list while iterating over it.** - **Bare `except:`**, hiding real bugs. - **Forgetting `self`** in a method signature. - **Deeply nested comprehensions** that a loop would express more clearly. - **Files opened without `with`**, leaking handles. - **Missing `encoding="utf-8"`**, crashing on non-ASCII characters. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: create a **`Dataset` class** storing records as a list of dictionaries, with **add, filter and summary methods and error handling**. Use the version above as a reference but write your own — and add `__len__` and `__repr__`, because implementing dunder methods is the moment classes stop feeling like syntax and start feeling like building blocks. The mini project is a **mini inventory system** with `Product` and `Inventory` classes that **reads from and writes to a JSON file**. The persistence requirement is what makes it real: your objects have to serialize to plain dictionaries and reconstruct from them, which is exactly the pattern you will use for saving model configurations and results later. For the assignment, **refactor Day 2's grade calculator into an OOP design with a `Student` class and exception handling**. Compare the two versions side by side and note what improved — usually it is that related data and behaviour now live together, and invalid states become impossible to construct rather than merely unlikely. That comparison is the clearest way to understand why the field uses objects. ##### Key takeaways - Choose structures by access pattern: lists for ordered sequences, tuples for fixed immutable groups, sets for fast membership and deduplication, dicts for key–value lookup. - Sets and dicts give O(1) membership testing; using a list instead is the difference between seconds and minutes at scale. - Comprehensions express map-and-filter in one readable line, and `{label: i}` mappings are a staple of every classification project. - Classes bundle data with behaviour; `__init__`, `self`, `super()` and dunder methods like `__len__` and `__repr__` are the mechanics every AI library relies on. - Catch specific exceptions at the level that can handle them, and always use `with open(..., encoding="utf-8")` for file access.
